source.title: How does Chain of Thought Think? Mechanistic Interpretability of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Sparse Autoencoding
source.authors: Xi Chen; A. Plaat; Niki van Stein

record.file_problem: none; full paper and appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: Extends evidence about sparse features to pretrained language models, using SAE feature extraction, activation measurements, and feature-level patching rather than toy-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The study reports SAE feature explanation scores, causal patching effects, residual-activation sparsity, and neuron counts per SAE feature. Reported patching outcomes and structural measurements are included; descriptions of earlier studies are not included.
record.test_reason: The study uses SAEs as a tool to compare CoT and NoCoT prompting in Pythia-70M and 2.8B, and it reports how that contrast changes explanation scores, patching effects and activation sparsity. No result bears on whether features are superposed, whether polysemanticity comes from capacity, or whether SAE features are canonical. Its superposition remark ('indirect mitigation of the superposition problem') is an untested appendix interpretation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but the framing is CoT faithfulness. Authors conclude CoT induces more interpretable, sparser, causally effective features in Pythia-2.8B, with minimal effect in 70M. The superposition-mitigation point is a speculative appendix interpretation, not a tested result. Limits are final-token, layer-2 only, LLM-based scoring, small models and SAE biases.
record.recipe_differences: This is a post-hoc analysis of pretrained language models using separate SAEs, feature-level activation patching, and sparsity measurements; it does not reproduce the original toy-network setup or its feature-sparsity and geometric sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Results differ by model size (Pythia-70M versus Pythia-2.8B), prompting condition (CoT versus NoCoT), dictionary ratio (4 versus 8), patch direction, and feature-selection scheme (Top-K versus Random-K).

fits_no_version.finding: In Pythia-2.8B, CoT prompting raises SAE explanation scores (0.056 vs -0.013, p=0.004), residual sparsity and per-feature neuron concentration. Effects are weak or absent in 70M. Authors speculate this mitigates superposition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompting style (CoT) changes activation sparsity and SAE-feature interpretability, potentially reducing superposition, in larger LMs.

fits_no_version.finding: Patching CoT SAE features into NoCoT runs raises correct-answer log-prob in 2.8B (about +2.4 to +3.2), but not in 70M, where it is negative. Random-K often beats Top-K.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features from CoT runs causally transfer reasoning benefit in larger but not smaller models.

record.problems: Evidence is restricted to two Pythia models, one residual-stream layer, final-token activations, and the GSM8K training split. Many sparsity and patching results are presented only in figures without numeric values or reported error bars. Explanation scores rely on an LLM-based scoring method, and the authors note SAE analysis may miss distributed or entangled representations.
record.rows_left_out: No separately quantified outcomes beyond those recorded are stated for the feature-count plots; the reported comparisons are represented by one row per model and prompt contrast. The study's general reasoning-performance statements are not entered as separate rows because they do not measure the claimed feature geometry.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep or geometry.
No test of capacity competition or dedicated dimensions.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
SAEs are used as a tool. The study does not test whether features are distributed across neurons or whether SAEs recover genuine sparse features.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicity. Authors note SAEs may miss distributed or entangled representations.

record.verdict_notes: Not a test of superposition. Explanation scores are near zero in both conditions, which, if anything, questions SAE feature interpretability here, but the study never evaluates that. Rows r13 and r14 compare the study's own selection schemes.

versions.untested_parts: No small toy networks, feature-over-dimension sweep, or toy-model geometry is tested.
The study does not test whether neuron polysemanticity results from capacity competition or whether important features obtain dedicated dimensions.
The study does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
The study examines two Pythia models, one layer, and final-token activations; it does not establish how widespread these findings are across LLM families, layers, or tasks.
It does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units; the authors note SAE analyses can miss distributed or entangled representations.
The study does not test whether the underlying features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE feature explanation scores for features learned from CoT and NoCoT activations.
rows.locator: Table 1; Effect of CoT on Feature Interpretability
rows.note: The text describes the difference as slight and not statistically significant; the figure's median and outliers favor NoCoT.
rows.check: CoT vs NoCoT explanation-score contrast. It measures a prompting effect, not whether SAEs recover sparse features (V4).

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8B
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE feature explanation scores for features learned from CoT and NoCoT activations.
rows.uncertainty: CoT Std 0.147; NoCoT Std 0.071; t = 2.96, p = 0.004
rows.locator: Table 1; Effect of CoT on Feature Interpretability
rows.note: The paper reports higher explanation scores under CoT and calls the difference statistically significant.
rows.check: Same CoT vs NoCoT contrast. Absolute scores are very low (mean 0.056 vs -0.013), and the study does not assess these as feature recovery.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Patched the top 20 CoT features into NoCoT runs and measured the change in correct-answer log-probability.
rows.locator: Figure 3 / Appendix Figure 10; Causal Effects of CoT Features via Activation Patching
rows.note: Text describes highly variable effects, including large gains and losses, and says transfer is not reliable.
rows.check: Patching effect on answer log-prob measures CoT faithfulness or transfer, not superposition.

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8B
rows.operation_detail: Patched the top 20 CoT features into NoCoT runs and measured the change in correct-answer log-probability.
rows.locator: Figure 3 / Appendix Figure 10; Causal Effects of CoT Features via Activation Patching
rows.note: The text describes a strong positive shift and consistent improvement.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Patched the top 20 CoT features into NoCoT runs and measured the change in correct-answer log-probability.
rows.locator: Figure 4 / Appendix Figure 11; Causal Effects of CoT Features via Activation Patching
rows.note: The text reports high variance and frequent negative effects, with no stable transfer.

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8B

rows.locator: Figure 4 / Appendix Figure 11; Causal Effects of CoT Features via Activation Patching

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Gradually patched Top-K CoT features into NoCoT runs.
rows.measure: Change in correct-answer log-probability across patch curve
rows.value: No gain; curve declines steadily after K > 4, eventually around -8 log-prob
rows.note: The paper reports a decline rather than a benefit from transferring CoT features.
rows.check: Patch-curve result on a CoT-transfer construct. Reversed refers to the CoT benefit, not any version.

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8B
rows.operation_detail: Gradually patched Top-K CoT features into NoCoT runs.
rows.measure: Change in correct-answer log-probability across patch curve
rows.value: Over +2.5 log-prob at K = 2, then gradually declines to around +1.8
rows.note: The text describes a strong early gain that remains positive as more features are patched.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Gradually patched Top-K CoT features into NoCoT runs.
rows.measure: Change in correct-answer log-probability across patch curve
rows.value: Curve remains below zero; minimum drop about -3
rows.note: The paper says the effect is less severe than at ratio 4, but remains negative.

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8B
rows.operation_detail: Gradually patched Top-K CoT features into NoCoT runs.
rows.measure: Change in correct-answer log-probability across patch curve
rows.value: Exceeds +3.2 at K = 2, then stabilizes at approximately +2.4
rows.note: The text describes positive transfer with diminishing returns.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Patched NoCoT features into CoT runs.
rows.measure: Change in correct-answer log-probability across patch curve
rows.value: Approximately +3 at K = 2, diminishing and stabilizing around +1 near K = 128
rows.note: This reverse-direction result is described as a fragile advantage, not a consistent CoT-to-NoCoT feature-transfer benefit.
rows.check: Reverse-direction patch. Its state was graded against a CoT hypothesis, not a version.

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8B
rows.operation_detail: Patched NoCoT features into CoT runs.
rows.measure: Change in correct-answer log-probability across patch curve
rows.value: Curve largely flat; slight interference may occur
rows.note: The text says this reverse patch has little to no benefit.

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8B
rows.operation_detail: Compared random-K feature selection with Top-K feature selection for CoT-to-NoCoT patching.
rows.value: Random-K often outperforms Top-K; numeric values figure only
rows.locator: Figures 5-6; Figures 12-13; Extended Analysis of Results
rows.note: Authors interpret this as useful CoT information being distributed across more than the strongest-activation features.
rows.check: Random-K vs Top-K compares the study's own feature-selection schemes; it should not be a claim row. Also, the abstract example 1.2 to 4.3 is not recorded.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Compared random-K and Top-K feature selection for CoT-to-NoCoT patching.
rows.value: Neither random nor Top-K patching consistently improves performance; numeric values figure only
rows.locator: Figures 5-6; Figures 12-13; Extended Analysis of Results
rows.note: The text says both selection schemes fail to consistently improve performance in this model.
rows.check: Selection-scheme comparison of the study's own method, as in r13.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Compared residual-stream activation sparsity under CoT and NoCoT prompts.
rows.measure: Proportion of residual activations close to zero
rows.baseline: NoCoT: broader activation distribution, more neurons with moderate-to-high activation
rows.value: CoT: significantly sparser distribution, with most activations low and a few strong
rows.locator: Figure 7; Appendix Figure 14; Activation Sparsity under CoT and NoCoT
rows.note: The text reports the effect in both models and says it is more pronounced in the larger model.
rows.check: Residual sparsity under CoT vs NoCoT is activation sparsity per prompt, not a measure of superposition or feature recovery.

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8B
rows.operation_detail: Compared residual-stream activation sparsity under CoT and NoCoT prompts.
rows.measure: Proportion of residual activations close to zero
rows.baseline: NoCoT: heavier tail and more neurons with high activation
rows.value: CoT: almost all activations low except a small subset
rows.locator: Figure 7; Appendix Figure 14; Activation Sparsity under CoT and NoCoT
rows.note: The text calls the sparsity effect markedly more pronounced in this model.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Compared the number of neurons activated per SAE feature under CoT and NoCoT.
rows.measure: Activated neuron counts per SAE feature
rows.baseline: NoCoT features activate a broader set of neurons
rows.value: CoT features tend to activate a smaller number of neurons
rows.note: The text characterizes CoT features as more concentrated, but says the feature-level sparsification is weaker than in Pythia-2.8B.
rows.check: Neuron counts per SAE feature are compared across prompts only. No baseline shows features are spread across neurons because of superposition.

rows.subject: Pythia-2.8B
rows.operation_detail: Compared the number of neurons activated per SAE feature under CoT and NoCoT.
rows.measure: Activated neuron counts per SAE feature
rows.baseline: NoCoT features activate relatively large numbers of neurons
rows.value: CoT features are supported by very small subsets of neurons; feature-level variance is higher
rows.note: The authors describe a more pronounced structured-sparsity pattern in the larger model.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Pythia-2.8B under CoT prompting on GSM8K
reader_labels.reason: CoT SAE features have higher explanation scores, feature-level neuron counts are more concentrated, and patching them into NoCoT runs improves answer log-probability (r2, r4, r6, r8, r10, r16, r18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Pythia-70M under CoT prompting on GSM8K
reader_labels.reason: Residual and SAE-feature sparsity is reported, but explanation scores show no significant CoT advantage and CoT-to-NoCoT feature patches do not reliably help and can reduce log-probability (r1, r3, r5, r7, r9, r15, r17).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The positive transfer is not confined to the top-ranked features; random selection often performs better, so the result does not show that a small set of top features captures the useful information (r13).
